1:
The demand is unchanged, and Henry makes that the point: Let my people go was still the whole of it, and the trial is simply whose word shall stand. He hears the reasonableness in the possessive — they are my people, therefore let them go — and the jealousy in what it will cost, since God will give Egypt for their ransom rather than leave Israel undelivered. Calvin finds the same defiance in the title: the Lord God of the Hebrews is no unmeaning repetition but a taunt, teaching Pharaoh that the God he thought he had repelled was still in the field against him, and convicting him of sacrilege twice over, in oppressing God's people and in defrauding God of his honour. Clarke reads the two divine names apart, taking the first for eternal power and Godhead and the second in the sense of Supporter and Defender.

What follows is a stroke without an instrument. Henry and Wesley both notice that the hand of the Lord falls on the cattle immediately, without Aaron's rod being stretched out, and both draw the same lesson, that God's hand is to be acknowledged in the sickness and death of beasts, since a sparrow does not fall to the ground without our Father. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the Hebrew for the plague as that which sweeps away. Calvin adds that calling it God's hand sets it against natural causes and accidental chances alike, and observes that though this plague looks lighter than those before it, it was heavier in its consequences: earlier the evil had been removed with the infliction, whereas dead herds would impoverish Egypt for years — a gradation he sees threatened in the law itself.

The exemption of Israel is what the commentators dwell on. Gill calls it a marvellous separation, the Hebrew cattle breathing the same air and feeding in the same pastures untouched; Ellicott observes that Israel had shared the first three plagues, which brought annoyance but no loss, and dates their exemption from here. He also explains why the timing mattered: murrain is not uncommon in Egypt, especially in the Delta, so God marked this one as his by fixing a day, by sparing Israel's herds, and by striking every Egyptian beast left in the field — and the day's delay, he notes, gave any Egyptian who believed Moses time to bring his cattle under cover. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point about the appointed hour.

Then the difficulty. The text says all the cattle of Egypt died, and later verses plainly assume that cattle survived. Calvin calls the phrase a synecdoche, meaning that the herds were everywhere destroyed and the murrain general, not that no animal remained. Keil and Delitzsch take all in its popular sense, as denoting a quantity beside which the remainder was nothing, and restrict it to the beasts in the field. Clarke resolves it differently again, reading it as all the cattle that died were Egyptian, and finds the proof in the next plague, which needed living animals to smite. He also draws the sharpest inference of the chapter: the Egyptians must have seen the vanity of their whole national worship when the animals they held sacred and deified were slain without distinction among the common herd, and wonders that animal worship could ever afterwards maintain its ground. Henry says the same more briefly, that what we make an idol of God justly removes.

Pharaoh's enquiry closes the plague and hardens him. Gill reports the Targum's guess that he sent as far as Pelusium; Clarke thinks he meant to replace his losses out of Hebrew stock; Henry allows him no better motive than curiosity or reprisal, and observes that an enquiry with no good design left him unmoved by its own answer. Calvin sees a man compelled to learn what he would gladly have gone on not knowing.
8:
The instrument of this plague is what the commentators seize on first, because it fits the crime. Henry observes that when the death of their cattle had not moved them, God sent a plague that seized their own bodies — if lesser judgments fail, greater follow — and finds the signal significant: warm ashes flung toward heaven, after which a scalding dew came down and blistered where it fell. Sometimes, he says, God shows men their sin in their punishment. They had oppressed Israel in the furnaces, and now the ashes of the furnace were made as much a terror to them as ever their taskmasters had been to the Israelites. Clarke makes the same point from the brick-kilns, every particle of that unjust labour seeming to become a boil upon the king; and Ellicott notes it was probably a brick-kiln, since much of Goshen had been turned into a brick-field. Their own wrongdoing became the whip with which God scourged them.

What the disease was gets careful attention. Keil and Delitzsch derive the two Hebrew words from roots meaning to be hot and to swell up, and identify the natural substratum with the Nile-blisters, which come out as small pimples on reddened skin and turn quickly into round crowded blisters — a summer rash appearing toward the close of the inundation, which the Egyptians call the heat of the Nile. Clarke calls it one of the most poignant afflictions short of death: if a single boil throws the whole system into a fever, what must a multitude at once occasion? He reports an old chronicler's account that the blisters burst with tormenting pain and bred worms. Wesley describes it as a burning scab. Ellicott concedes such complaints are not uncommon in Egypt, but insists they are seldom severe and do not fall indifferently on man and beast, and lists four marks of the miracle: it was announced beforehand, severe, universal, and reached the animals.

The magicians are routed here, and everyone enjoys it. Gill notes that though they had attempted no imitation since the lice, they had stayed about Pharaoh belittling the miracles. Calvin says that Satan, though ten times conquered, is hurried on with indefatigable obstinacy, and his ministers with him: these men had already confessed their art could go no further, yet emboldened themselves to try all extremities until the boils drove them back in disgrace. Ellicott suspects they had come expressly to withstand Moses. Henry itemises the justice of it — they were punished for helping to harden Pharaoh's heart and for making sport of the former plagues, so that those who would produce lice were made against their wills to produce boils; it is ill jesting with God's judgments, he says, and more dangerous than playing with fire. They were shamed before their own admirers, since enchantments that cannot secure their owners are weak indeed. Clarke observes that they could neither imitate the plague nor remove it from their own tormented flesh, and that they are never mentioned again.

The hardening then changes hands, and this is the hinge. Henry, Wesley and Ellicott all mark that up to now Pharaoh had hardened his own heart, and that God now hardens it: wilful hardness, Henry says, is commonly punished with judicial hardness, and if men shut their eyes against the light it is just with God to close them — a judgment he calls the sorest on this side hell. Ellicott sets it beside the apostle's account of the heathen given over to a reprobate mind. Calvin presses furthest, refusing to soften the phrase into foreknowledge: when the text says as the Lord had spoken it claims both the effect and the foresight for God, and yet the tyrant is not absolved, his hardness being voluntary. Calvin notices in passing that boils breaking out on cattle prove not every beast had died before.
13:
The demand is made a seventh time, and Henry sees the difficulty in that: God has just hardened the heart, and still requires obedience of it. He reads the requirement as itself a punishment, fitted to a king who had demanded bricks while denying straw. Calvin agrees that no cure is expected — God returns to threats not in hope but so that the obstinacy may be more openly discovered; it was worth having such a picture set before us, since nobody would otherwise believe a man could resist God so. Gill takes the promised plagues upon the heart to mean everything God had determined, and Wesley notes that Pharaoh had not yet felt any stroke in his own person. Henry gives the phrase its sharpest turn: God can plague the heart either by making it senseless or by making it hopeless, and those are the worst plagues of all. Calvin says the strokes must now reach the bowels, since it was not enough to batter this man's sides, and Ellicott describes the blows as meant to beat the heart down until it should yield and let the whole people go. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the closing reproach as a military image, the king damming himself up like a rampart against God's people.

Then comes a sentence that says something which never happened, and three voices converge on the same repair. God declares that he will smite Pharaoh with pestilence and cut him off from the earth; yet Gill observes flatly that we never find this was done. It cannot well be the death of the firstborn, since it is not certain that was pestilence and Pharaoh himself was not smitten. Gill therefore reads the verbs as past — if now I had stretched out my hand — placing the moment at the murrain. Clarke argues the same more forcefully: the Hebrew verbs are past, and our future creates the contradiction; rendered as a condition contrary to fact, it vanishes. Ellicott concedes the words admit a future rendering but rules that the context forbids it.

The verse that follows is the celebrated one, and here the agreement breaks. All parties accept that the word means God caused Pharaoh to stand. Ellicott takes it as kept thee alive — not for thy deserts, not even in pity, but only to show my power in thee. Gill reads it as preservation from the earlier plagues and reservation for greater judgments. Calvin canvasses the renderings, notes that the Greek extended it to I have stirred thee up, and prefers preservation: had Pharaoh fallen in one trifling engagement the glory of the victory would have been less illustrious, so God delayed the stroke that the tyrant might slowly learn how vainly he strove. But Calvin will not stop there. Behind the long-suffering stands eternal prescience: God spared Pharaoh to stand for a time because before he was born he had been predestinated to this purpose. Those who use the verse to overturn predestination mistake it, he adds, since the text does not say God created him with this intention but that he suspended judgment, Pharaoh being the instrument of his wrath.

Clarke attacks precisely that reading. He renders the clause as caused thee to subsist, insists that judicious critics of almost all creeds agree, and argues that neither the Hebrew, nor Paul's rendering, nor the Greek can countenance what he calls a most exceptionable meaning — that God appointed this man from eternity and hardened him to display power in destroying him. So man speaks, Clarke says; thus God has not spoken. Wesley makes the distinction most cleanly: granting that Pharaoh was marked for ruin and providentially given to Moses as an adversary fierce enough to make the victory memorable, he adds that this was the event, and it by no means follows it was the design.
18:
The hail is announced for a named hour, and that precision is what the commentators fasten on. Clarke says the time was fixed so circumstantially in order to teach Pharaoh that Jehovah is Lord of heaven and earth, and that water, fire, earth and air — every one an object of Egyptian worship — were creatures of his power and now instruments of Egypt's destruction. Calvin builds an argument out of the same fact. Hail does sometimes destroy corn, he grants, so much so that fifteen years without such a calamity counts as a blessing; but five marks show this one was not natural. The day was named, and not the day only but the hour — and what astronomer, he asks, can measure out the moments for a storm? Then its violence was such as had never been seen; then its extent, running the whole length and breadth of Egypt, whereas ordinary tempests fly like an arrow within narrow limits; and last, the exemption of Goshen. It was no accidental impulse, he concludes, and no mere freezing of moisture in mid air, but a portent transcending the bounds of nature.

Clarke goes the other way and explains the mechanism. To rain hail is exactly correct, he says, since drops falling through a cold region freeze as they descend, and a stone grows larger the farther it falls by gathering the water it meets; if natural means were used at all, he supposes a highly electrified atmosphere heavy with vapour. He then piles up modern parallels — a storm near Liverpool whose stones measured five inches round, and an Italian tempest reported to have killed the beasts, the birds and even the fish. His conclusion is not naturalistic at all: the Almighty asks Job whether he has seen the treasures of the hail, and while God has such artillery at command, how soon may he desolate a country or a world. Ellicott supplies the local measure: rain and hail are not unknown in Lower Egypt, but thunderstorms are rare and usually harmless, one that killed a man being thought so remarkable that it spread universal consternation. Wesley glosses the comparison simply, that Egypt is dated from its founding as a kingdom.

Then comes the warning to house the cattle, and here the readings split. Gill takes it for pure clemency, showing how certain and how terrible the plague would be, and how in the midst of wrath God remembers mercy. Clarke says the same in a sentence, adding that every life might have been saved had the warning been heeded. Keil and Delitzsch make it a theological hinge: the advice was a sign of divine mercy that would still have rescued the hardened man, and its being given proves that submission remained possible, the hardening not yet being complete. Ellicott shows how practicable it was, since Egypt's yearly inundation meant shelter for cattle was abnormally plentiful, every beast having to be gathered into sheds beside the mounded villages — so housing what the murrain had left would have been easy. Calvin alone hears no mercy in it. God does not counsel as one who would spare a professed enemy, he says, but insults the king's mad confidence, hinting that now at last is the time for fear; the challenge is issued openly because when God contends the event is not doubtful, and he may grant a way of escape and still be certain of victory.
22:
The storm is summoned by the rod, and Henry takes the obedience of the elements for the lesson: fire and hail fulfil God's word. He makes the clouds serve two offices — storehouses out of which God drops fatness upon his people, and magazines out of which he draws artillery against his enemies — recalling the treasures of hail that Job is asked about. Calvin asks why the rod was used at all, since Moses had already predicted the hail before he was told how it would come. He suspects the command followed the prediction, and finds in that a trial of his servant's faith; the gesture served less for Pharaoh than for Moses, who was to be encouraged for the contests ahead by seeing his commission renewed. What we should learn from it, Calvin adds, is that the elements, senseless as they are, stand ready to obey their Maker.

The fire is the strange part. Clarke notes that the word for thunder is properly voices, meaning loud repeated peals, and insists that what the English renders running along the ground is literally the fire walked upon the earth — no sudden flash but a devouring fire moving through every part, its progress irresistible. Ellicott gives the same rendering and reports the dispute: some take it for ordinary lightning, others hold the phenomenon was what the Version suggests, and he inclines to the latter, observing that the electric fluid does occasionally take a form with something of permanency, lasting seconds or minutes — the appearances called fire-balls, which mark an extreme disturbance and great peril to life. If that phrase does not imply as much, the next surely does, for the fire is described as infolding itself in the midst of the hail. Gill quotes the rabbinic verdict that this was a miracle within a miracle, since the hail did not quench the fire nor the fire melt the hail. Clarke observes that the electric fluid is essential to hail in any case, and that here it was supplied in supernatural abundance.

On the extent of the ruin the grammarians restrain the language. Keil and Delitzsch warn that every herb and every tree are not to be taken absolutely, any more than all the cattle earlier; and Ellicott agrees, explaining that the hail broke off small boughs and twigs rather than shattering great trees, so destroying the prospect of fruit, and adding that a storm like this would have levelled everything more than a few inches high. Keil and Delitzsch then set out what was and was not unusual: storms are uncommon in Lower and Middle Egypt but do occur between December and April, sometimes with hail, though rarely severe; and they came at the season when they come, when the cattle are in the field, that being the only part of the year when Egyptian cattle are put out to pasture. What marked this storm as supernatural was its prediction, the exemption of Goshen, and above all a fury which impressed Pharaoh more than every plague before it. Henry sees the same selectivity in the corn: what stood above ground was destroyed and only what had not risen was spared, God having many ways of taking away the corn in its season.

Goshen's exemption draws the usual remark and one unusual one. Clarke calls it a signal proof of a most particular providence. Henry observes that God directs the pregnant clouds and causes it to rain or hail on one city and not another, in mercy or in judgment as he pleases. Gill notices something the others pass over: any Egyptians living among the Israelites escaped with them, their servants and cattle and fruits untouched — and he draws the general rule that wicked men often fare the better for the people of God who live among them.
27:
Pharaoh's confession is the strongest words he ever uses. Clarke notes that the Hebrew is emphatic in a way the English loses: the Lord is the Righteous One, and I and my people are the Sinners — he alone just, we alone transgressors — and asks who could have imagined that after such an acknowledgment the man would harden himself again. Ellicott adds that Pharaoh had previously denounced the Israelites as idlers, whereas now he blames only himself and his people; the confession is satisfactory except that it divides a guilt almost wholly his own. He explains the change by the plague's severity, and by the storm still going on with no sign of ending. Calvin agrees that as far as words go this is true repentance, and draws the rule that sinners honour God's justice only by condemning themselves.

But Calvin will not grant the thing itself. Had the confession come from the heart it would have been repentance, but fear in a wicked heart is no governing principle; and yet, he insists, Pharaoh was not deliberately lying. Seized by terror, a man catches at any means of appeasing God; under necessity the wicked will promise anything, and then, because what they promised was extorted, break out afresh once the fear is gone. He finds the pattern in Saul, who confessed David's innocence and hunted him again as soon as the danger passed. Even the plea Calvin reads as terror rather than conviction: the words rendered for it is enough have been variously construed, and he rejects the reading that has Pharaoh congratulating himself that the thunder has stopped, preferring a man beaten down by the rolling of the storm and offering that as evidence of a conversion he cannot otherwise prove. Gill gives the alternatives — that there has been enough of hail and thunder, or a prayer that this be reckoned enough, or an appeal to pray without intermission until it ceases. Clarke hears simple surrender, and glosses the mighty thunderings as voices of God, a Hebrew superlative like mountains of God for very high mountains.

Moses answers that he will pray once outside the city. Gill reports the rabbinic explanation that the city was full of idols, but prefers privacy, adding that Moses may also have wished to show he did not fear the storm. Calvin makes the departure a judgment on the place: Moses must leave Pharaoh's presence to supplicate purely, since the king's unbelief would pollute the offering. Ellicott explains what the promised knowledge was for: Egyptians believed every country had its own gods, and Pharaoh had come only so far as to treat Jehovah as the God of the Hebrews, whereas the point was to have him owned as God of the whole earth. Calvin allows that the word may mean Egypt or the world, and cares more for the argument — that God's dominion appears not only when he avenges but when the elements serve his mercy, and most clearly when he heals the wounds he inflicted.

Moses then tells the king plainly that he and his servants do not yet fear the Lord, and Calvin admires the nerve of it: nothing but a miraculous restraint, he thinks, kept the court from killing a man who condemned them to their faces. The distinction drawn is between alarm and reverence — true fear attaches a man to God and is the beginning of wisdom, whereas hypocrites may dread God's name and have no wish to serve him. That raises his last question. Why intercede where no repentance appears? Because Moses did not mean to spare, but granted an interval in which the king's impiety would betray itself again, so that God might fulfil what he had said about all the plagues. It is absurd, Calvin concludes, to infer from this that ministers should be content with a merely verbal confession.
31:
The note about the crops is short, and the commentators make it carry a great deal. Ellicott treats it as a dating device: flax forms its seed-vessel toward the end of January and barley comes into ear about the same time, so these facts fix the date of this plague and help fix the others. Keil and Delitzsch read the same verses as an accounting of loss, showing how much had gone and how much remained: flax and barley were not yet ripe but in ear and blossom, and so were broken, while the later grain had no ears to break. Clarke supplies the fuller agricultural picture from a traveller's report of Egypt's double seed-time and harvest — the summer grains sown in March before the inundation and reaped about October, wheat and barley sown once the Nile has fallen and reaped before May.

The second grain is disputed. Gill reports the opinion that it is rice, rye being scarcely known there and growing too quickly. Clarke derives the Hebrew from a root meaning to have long hair, making it some bearded grain, canvasses the versions which give spelt, and confesses that what it means cannot positively be said; he notes that one old translator, probably baffled, left the verse out. Ellicott is the most decided: rye is a wrong translation for a grain never grown in Egypt, the only three cultivated being wheat, barley and the sorghum called doora, which he takes the Hebrew to mean. He explains the escape by the calendar — wheat comes into ear a full month after barley — the ear still hidden in low tufts that grew like grass. Calvin draws the moral instead: God destroyed what had grown into stalk and spared what came on more slowly, leaving a remnant of hope which might invite the king to repentance, if his wickedness were curable.

Moses then goes out into the storm to pray. Gill has him retire into the field; Clarke guesses the rod was in the outspread hands; Wesley repeats that he went to show he dared venture abroad under hail and lightning, and adds that his prayer opened and shut heaven as Elijah's did — yet neither could subdue a hard heart. Ellicott quotes a modern description of the prophet standing bareheaded under the tempestuous canopy of heaven, safe though all around might be destroyed, since the very hairs of his head were numbered.

The relapse follows at once, and the chapter ends where the argument began. Gill observes that instead of being softened the heart grew harder as soon as the plague lifted. Calvin makes it a rule of the reprobate mind: security arms men against God, so that as soon as the scourges rest they take a short truce for a settled peace — and Moses aggravates the crime at the close by recording that he had foretold this very obstinacy. Ellicott observes that since Pharaoh had never been so deeply moved before, it now cost a greater effort of will to harden himself, so that he sinned more in doing it than yet. Clarke ends with the argument he has been building throughout. These acts were merely Pharaoh's own; the hardening verbs often carry no more than permission, so that God suffered his heart to be hardened; and his heart is said to harden only after each miracle was seen and each plague removed, everything God did being fitter to soften than to harden. He lay under no fatal necessity and might have humbled himself; but he would sin, and therefore had to be punished. And Clarke turns it on the reader: this man sinned against a comparatively unknown God, whereas those who do the same with the Bible in their hands sin against far more, so that Pharaoh hardening himself against ten plagues looks almost a saint beside men hardening themselves against ten millions of mercies.
